vignette:
Mai was 24 years old, a slender woman with a quiet, watchful presence that colleagues at the city planning office sometimes mistook for shyness. She had been an urban planner for two years, spending her days analyzing traffic flow and pedestrian access in a mid-sized Midwestern city. But the work that required her full attention-reading density reports, zoning maps, public feedback forms-had become increasingly difficult. Her concentration would fray without warning. She would be staring at a spreadsheet and suddenly realize she had been holding her breath, or that her stomach had tightened into a knot, and she could not remember the last three minutes of what she had read.

The memory of what her mother had done to her lived in Mai's body, not in her mind. When she tried deliberately to recall the details-the exact words, the sequence of events, the room she was in-the memory slipped away like water through fingers. She could not reconstruct it on command. But sometimes, without any image or warning, the full emotional weight of it would crash over her. She would be standing at the bus stop, or sitting in a coffee shop, and suddenly she was flooded with a rage so pure and hot it frightened her. There was no picture in her head, only the feeling: a white-hot fury at the injustice of what had been done to her, and the knowledge that nothing had ever been done about it. Her mother had never apologized. No one had intervened. The abuse had simply stopped when Mai grew old enough to resist, and the silence that followed was as complete as if it had never happened.

Mai had come to believe, without ever saying it aloud, that she was not quite a person. She felt like an object-something to be used, moved, ignored. The feeling was strongest when she was seen by others. Being noticed, being looked at, made her skin crawl. She had learned to make herself small. At work, she agreed with whatever her supervisor suggested, even when she had a better idea. She said yes to extra assignments she did not want. She stayed late because she could not bring herself to say no. It felt safer to go along. She had developed a quiet theory about this: if she was agreeable enough, if she never made anyone angry, no one would ever hurt her again. She knew, somewhere, that this was not rational, but the feeling was stronger than the thought.

Her world had shrunk. She felt safe in only a handful of places: her apartment, a specific corner of the library, the back booth of a diner she went to on Sunday mornings. Anywhere else, she was on guard. Sudden movements from other people-a hand reaching across a table, a person turning quickly in a hallway-made her flinch internally, her whole body bracing. She did not flinch visibly anymore; she had trained herself out of that. But the alertness was exhausting.

Medical appointments had become impossible. The thought of lying still while someone examined her, touched her, made her feel nauseous. She had cancelled her annual physical three times. The nausea itself had become a trigger. If she felt queasy for any reason-a bad meal, a stomach bug-it looped back into the old fear, and she would find herself trembling without knowing why.

What finally brought Mai to therapy was a meeting at work. A senior planner had gestured broadly while speaking, and the sudden movement had made Mai lose her train of thought entirely. She had sat frozen, unable to answer a direct question, feeling the eyes of six colleagues on her. She had excused herself to the bathroom and stood over the sink, shaking. She could not keep living like this. She was not sure she could change, but she knew she could not continue.
